questions.question:
D1 — Reuse the job library's retry hooks or roll a custom scheduler?
Project/branch/task: main branch, retry-framework plan; adding retries to 5 background workers.
ELI10: The job library you already use has retry hooks built in, and your plan says your custom version would be "the same shape." Building your own copy inside each worker means five hand-written schedulers to keep correct, versus configuring one curve the library already knows how to run. The plan's reason for going custom is "full control over the curve," and most retry hook APIs give you that through a backoff callback.
Stakes if we pick wrong: five bespoke schedulers drift apart, each grows its own bugs (no jitter, no cap, retry storms), and nobody at 3am knows which curve a given worker actually runs.
Recommendation: A because the plan admits the library version has the same shape, and a custom curve is usually a config callback, not a new scheduler.
Completeness: A=9/10, B=5/10, C=n/a (investigation, decides nothing)
Pros / cons:
A) Library hooks + custom curve (recommended)
  ✅ One scheduler the library already tests; the curve becomes a per-worker config function (human: ~1 day / CC: ~20 min)
  ✅ Attempt-count persistence, max attempts and dead-letter usually come along for free with the hooks
  ❌ If the hook API cannot accept an arbitrary curve function, that is a new fact and R1 reopens
B) Custom inline scheduler (as planned)
  ✅ Total control of delay math and logging, independent of the library's release cycle
  ✅ No dependency on hook semantics nobody has read yet (human: ~3 days / CC: ~1 hr)
  ❌ Five hand-rolled schedulers to keep in sync, plus reimplementing attempt persistence and terminal handling
C) Investigate first: bounded read of the hook API
  ✅ Settles "can the hooks take a custom curve" with evidence before committing either way
  ✅ Cheap: ~30 min human / ~3 min CC reading the hook signature and docs
  ❌ Decides nothing; R1 stays pending and the review pauses on this question
Net: You are trading a library dependency you already carry for five copies of scheduler code you would own forever.

options.label: Library hooks + custom curve (recommended)
options.description: Use the job library's built-in retry hooks; supply each worker's backoff curve as a callback/config. One scheduler the library already tests. Attempt persistence, max attempts and dead-letter usually included. Human ~1 day / CC ~20 min. Risk: if the hook API cannot take an arbitrary curve, R1 reopens. Completeness 9/10.

options.label: Custom inline scheduler (as planned)
options.description: Roll the exponential-backoff scheduler inline in each of the 5 workers as PLAN.md:7-9 proposes. Total control of delay math and logging. Human ~3 days / CC ~1 hr. Cost: five schedulers to keep in sync, plus attempt persistence and terminal handling rebuilt by hand. Completeness 5/10.

options.label: Investigate hook API first
options.description: Bounded ~30 min human / ~3 min CC read of the library's retry hook signature and docs, then return to this question. Approves nothing; R1 stays pending; R2–R6 unchanged.

questions.question:
D2 — What delivery guarantee does processWebhookJob() keep once it can retry?
Project/branch/task: main branch, retry-framework plan; the webhook worker is one of the 5 workers gaining retries through library hooks (D1).
ELI10: Today the webhook worker sends each event at most once: if the send fails or times out, the event is dropped, never duplicated. A retry cannot tell "the request never arrived" apart from "it arrived but the response got lost," so any retry after a timeout can deliver the same event twice. Adding retries silently flips the guarantee from at-most-once to at-least-once. That is a contract change your webhook receivers depend on, and the plan does not name it.
Stakes if we pick wrong: receivers that are not idempotent process duplicate events (double emails, double charges, double state transitions); or, if we keep dropping on ambiguity, the retry framework never fixes the webhook worker's lost events.
Recommendation: B because losing events is usually worse than duplicates, and a stable idempotency key makes duplicates safe for receivers; this is still a contract call you know better than the review does.
Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score.
Pros / cons:
A) Keep at-most-once: retry only provably-unsent failures
  ✅ No duplicate deliveries ever; existing receivers keep working with no change on their side
  ✅ Still recovers the clear cases: connection refused, DNS failure, local enqueue error (human: ~1 day / CC: ~30 min)
  ❌ Timeouts and 5xx-after-send still drop events, so the biggest source of loss stays; needs per-attempt failure classification
B) Move to at-least-once with a stable idempotency key (recommended)
  ✅ Every event eventually reaches the receiver; retries after timeouts are safe because the event id stays constant across attempts
  ✅ Matches Stripe, Shopify and Svix practice; receivers dedupe on the key (human: ~1.5 days / CC: ~30 min incl. docs)
  ❌ Contract change: receivers must dedupe; needs a documented header, changelog entry and migration note for existing receivers
C) Exclude processWebhookJob() from retries
  ✅ Zero semantic change for receivers; the other 4 workers still get retries
  ✅ Smallest diff and no receiver communication (human: ~1 hr / CC: ~5 min)
  ❌ The webhook worker keeps losing events on every transient failure, which is likely why the plan touched it
Net: Never-duplicate-but-lossy, never-lossy-but-receivers-must-dedupe, or leave the webhook worker exactly as it is.

options.label: Keep at-most-once (retry only pre-send failures)
options.description: Webhook worker retries only failures provably raised before the request was written (connection refused, DNS, local error). Timeouts and 5xx-after-send still drop the event. No duplicates; receivers unchanged. Needs per-attempt failure classification. Human ~1 day / CC ~30 min.

options.label: At-least-once + idempotency key (recommended)
options.description: Webhook worker retries all transient failures; every delivery carries a stable event id / idempotency key header constant across attempts. Documented contract change with changelog and receiver migration note. Receivers dedupe on the key. Human ~1.5 days / CC ~30 min.

options.label: Exclude webhook worker from retries
options.description: `processWebhookJob()` keeps today's at-most-once, no-retry behavior; the other 4 workers retry via library hooks per D1. Smallest diff, no receiver impact, webhook events still lost on transient failure. Human ~1 hr / CC ~5 min.

questions.question:
D3 — When a job runs out of retries, where does it go?
Project/branch/task: main branch, retry-framework plan; retry bounds for all 5 workers running through library hooks (D1).
ELI10: Right now the plan describes the curve between retries but never says how many retries there are or what happens to a job that keeps failing. Without a limit, a poisoned job retries forever and eats worker capacity. With a limit but no landing spot, the job disappears with one log line nobody reads. A dead-letter store keeps the failed job, its payload reference and its last error so someone can inspect and replay it.
Stakes if we pick wrong: either an infinite-retry job starves the queue, or real work silently vanishes after the last attempt and the first sign is a customer asking where their data went.
Recommendation: A because a dead-letter store plus an alert is a few dozen lines with library hooks, and it turns "job vanished" into "job parked, here is why."
Completeness: A=10/10, B=5/10, C=3/10
Pros / cons:
A) Bounded attempts + dead-letter store + alert (recommended)
  ✅ Exhausted or fatal jobs are kept with last error and attempt history; operators can inspect and replay (human: ~1 day / CC: ~20 min)
  ✅ Metric and alert on dead-letter growth turns a silent failure into a page at the right time
  ❌ One more table or queue to own, plus a small replay path to build and test
B) Bounded attempts, log and drop
  ✅ Simplest bound: `maxAttempts` default 5 per worker, one error log on exhaustion (human: ~2 hr / CC: ~5 min)
  ✅ No new storage; nothing to operate
  ❌ Exhausted jobs are gone; recovery means replaying from upstream sources by hand, if that is even possible
C) Leave to library defaults
  ✅ Zero plan text and zero decision now
  ✅ Whatever the library does is at least consistent across the 5 workers
  ❌ Nobody knows the limit or the terminal behavior until an incident teaches them; 3am failure mode
Net: You are trading one small dead-letter store for never having to ask "where did that job go."

options.label: Bounded + dead-letter + alert (recommended)
options.description: `maxAttempts` default 5 with per-worker override. On exhaustion or fatal error the job lands in a dead-letter store (table or queue) with last error, attempt history and payload reference. Metric and alert on dead-letter growth. Manual replay path. Human ~1 day / CC ~20 min. Completeness 10/10.

options.label: Bounded, log and drop
options.description: `maxAttempts` default 5 with per-worker override. On exhaustion, log at error level with the last error and drop the job. No new storage, no replay. Human ~2 hr / CC ~5 min. Completeness 5/10.

options.label: Library defaults, unspecified
options.description: Do not write attempt limits or terminal behavior into the plan; accept whatever the library does by default. Completeness 3/10.

questions.question:
D4 — Should retry delays be randomized (jitter)?
Project/branch/task: main branch, retry-framework plan; the backoff curve each worker supplies to the library hooks (D1).
ELI10: When many jobs fail at the same moment because a shared dependency went down, a pure exponential curve makes them all retry at the same moments too, so the recovering dependency gets hit by a wave on every step. Jitter randomizes each job's delay so the retries spread out. It is one line inside the curve callback each worker already supplies.
Stakes if we pick wrong: synchronized retry waves knock a recovering dependency back over (the classic thundering herd); or, with jitter, per-job retry timing becomes slightly less predictable and tests need a seeded random source.
Recommendation: A because full jitter gives the least contention in AWS's published analysis and costs one line in a callback you are already writing.
Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score.
Pros / cons:
A) Full jitter: random(0, exponentialDelay) (recommended)
  ✅ Best spread of retries and lowest total contention after a shared outage (AWS Builders' Library)
  ✅ One line inside the D1 curve callback; RNG injected so tests stay deterministic (human: ~1 hr / CC: ~5 min)
  ❌ An individual retry can fire almost immediately; minimum wait is not guaranteed
B) Equal jitter: half fixed, half random
  ✅ Guarantees a minimum wait of half the exponential delay while still spreading retries
  ✅ Same one-line cost and same injectable RNG as full jitter (human: ~1 hr / CC: ~5 min)
  ❌ Slightly more contention than full jitter in the same analysis, and one more parameter to explain
C) No jitter: deterministic curve
  ✅ Fully deterministic; trivial to reason about and to assert exact delays in tests
  ✅ Zero extra code beyond the exponential curve
  ❌ Every job that failed together retries together; retry storms on recovery are the expected outcome
Net: One random() call now versus a synchronized retry wave the first time a dependency has a bad hour.

options.label: Full jitter (recommended)
options.description: delay = random(0, exponentialDelay) inside each worker's curve callback. Best spread, lowest contention. RNG injectable so tests are deterministic. Human ~1 hr / CC ~5 min.

options.label: Equal jitter
options.description: delay = exponentialDelay/2 + random(0, exponentialDelay/2). Guarantees a minimum wait; slightly more contention than full jitter. RNG injectable. Human ~1 hr / CC ~5 min.

options.label: No jitter
options.description: Deterministic exponential curve, no randomization. Simplest to test; retries synchronize after a shared outage.

questions.question:
D5 — Should the backoff delay have a ceiling?
Project/branch/task: main branch, retry-framework plan; the curve parameters each worker passes to the library hooks (D1, jittered per D4).
ELI10: Exponential backoff doubles the wait after each failure. That is fine for 5 attempts, but D3 lets each worker raise its attempt count, and a worker set to 15 attempts from a 1 second base would wait about 4.5 hours before its last try; at 20 attempts it would wait 6 days. A cap says "never wait longer than X between attempts," so the curve grows and then flattens. It is one min() call in the callback.
Stakes if we pick wrong: without a cap, a worker with a higher attempt count silently turns into a multi-day wait that looks like a stuck job; with a cap, one more number to document per worker.
Recommendation: A because the cap is one min() and it makes "how long can this job be delayed" a question with an answer.
Completeness: A=9/10, B=4/10
Pros / cons:
A) Cap each delay: default 10 min, per-worker override (recommended)
  ✅ Worst-case wait between attempts is bounded and documented for every worker (human: ~1 hr / CC: ~5 min)
  ✅ Also pins the curve defaults (base 1 s, multiplier 2) so all 5 workers start from the same documented numbers
  ❌ One more config value per worker to document and keep sane alongside maxAttempts
B) No cap
  ✅ Zero code; the curve is exactly the exponential the plan describes
  ✅ Fewer knobs to explain
  ❌ Any worker that raises maxAttempts past ~12 gets hour-to-day waits nobody intended
Net: One min() now versus a job that looks stuck for six days the first time someone bumps an attempt count.

options.label: Cap each delay (recommended)
options.description: delay = min(jitteredExponential, maxDelay). `maxDelay` default 10 minutes with per-worker override. Curve defaults documented: base 1 s, multiplier 2, per-worker override. Human ~1 hr / CC ~5 min. Completeness 9/10.

options.label: No cap
options.description: Raw exponential curve with no ceiling. Zero code, fewer knobs; high attempt counts produce hour-to-day waits. Completeness 4/10.

questions.question:
D6 — Which errors should the four non-webhook workers retry, and which go straight to dead-letter?
Project/branch/task: main branch, retry-framework plan; error handling inside the 4 non-webhook workers' library retry hooks (D1). The webhook worker's rule is already fixed by D2.
ELI10: Not every failure is worth retrying. A timeout or a "service busy" reply will likely pass on the next try. A validation error, a missing record or a bug that throws will fail the same way five times in a row, burning worker time and delaying the dead-letter record (D3) by the whole backoff curve. Classifying errors sends the hopeless ones to dead-letter immediately and spends retries only on the ones that can recover. The open question is what to do with an error nobody has classified yet.
Stakes if we pick wrong: either a bug retries five times per job across a whole queue before anyone sees it, or a transient error that nobody thought to list dead-letters real work on its first failure.
Recommendation: A because classification is a short list per worker, and defaulting unknown errors to retryable never loses work: the worst case is five wasted attempts, not a dropped job.
Completeness: A=10/10, B=5/10, C=8/10
Pros / cons:
A) Classify; unknown errors retry (recommended)
  ✅ Hopeless errors (validation, 4xx, missing record, TypeError) land in dead-letter on attempt 1 with the real cause visible (human: ~half day / CC: ~15 min)
  ✅ Unlisted errors still retry, so a forgotten transient class costs attempts, never data
  ❌ Each worker maintains a small error-class list, and a new fatal class retries needlessly until someone adds it
B) Retry everything until maxAttempts
  ✅ No lists to maintain; identical behavior in all 4 workers (human: ~0 / CC: ~0)
  ✅ Impossible to misclassify a transient error as fatal
  ❌ A deploy with a bug retries every affected job 5 times over the full curve before dead-lettering; queue capacity burns and diagnosis is delayed
C) Classify; unknown errors are fatal
  ✅ Zero wasted attempts on anything not explicitly known to be transient (human: ~half day / CC: ~15 min)
  ✅ Dead-letter fills fast, so new error classes surface quickly
  ❌ Any transient error missing from the list dead-letters real work on its first failure, which is the exact loss the retry framework exists to prevent
Net: A short list per worker plus a safe default, versus either wasted retries on bugs or lost work on unlisted transients.

options.label: Classify; unknown → retryable (recommended)
options.description: Each of the 4 workers declares retryable classes (timeout, connection error, 429/503, deadlock/serialization failure) and fatal classes (validation error, 4xx other than 429, missing record, programming error). Fatal → dead-letter immediately without consuming attempts. Unclassified errors retry. Human ~half day / CC ~15 min. Completeness 10/10.

options.label: Retry everything to maxAttempts
options.description: No classification. Every error consumes an attempt until `maxAttempts`, then dead-letter per D3. Zero code; bugs retry 5 times per job. Completeness 5/10.

options.label: Classify; unknown → fatal
options.description: Same declared classes as A, but unclassified errors go to dead-letter immediately. No wasted attempts; unlisted transient errors lose work on first failure. Human ~half day / CC ~15 min. Completeness 8/10.

questions.question:
D7 — One shared retry-policy module, or five copies and "refactor later"?
Project/branch/task: main branch, retry-framework plan; how the 5 workers carry the behavior approved in D3–D6.
ELI10: After D1 the library does the scheduling, but every worker still has to hand it the same four things: a jittered, capped curve, an error classifier, a dead-letter handoff and an attempt log line. The plan copies that block into five files and promises to clean up later. "Later" for copy-pasted retry code usually means the fifth copy drifts (no cap, wrong jitter) and nobody notices until an incident. The alternative is one small module that each worker configures with its own numbers and error lists.
Stakes if we pick wrong: five curves that silently disagree, five places to fix the next retry bug, and five test suites that each cover a slightly different subset; or, with a shared module, one bug that hits all five workers at once (mitigated by the module's own tests).
Recommendation: A because the behavior is identical by construction (D3–D6 fixed it), the module is under 100 lines, and it removes more lines than it adds while making the retry rules testable once.
Completeness: A=10/10, B=4/10, C=7/10
Pros / cons:
A) One shared retry-policy module (recommended)
  ✅ Curve, classifier, dead-letter handoff, attempt log and config validation are tested once and behave the same in all 5 workers (human: ~1 day / CC: ~20 min)
  ✅ Estimated 15–90 implementation lines saved; the helper's test suite replaces five near-duplicate suites
  ❌ A bug in the module reaches all 5 workers; the module's own tests are the guard
B) Five inline copies, refactor later (as planned)
  ✅ No shared dependency between workers; each can be changed in isolation (human: ~1.5 days / CC: ~30 min)
  ✅ Matches the plan text exactly; nothing new to name or place
  ❌ Five copies to keep in sync and five test suites to write; "later" rarely arrives for retry glue
C) Extract the curve builder only
  ✅ The math most likely to drift (jitter + cap) lives in one place (human: ~1 day / CC: ~15 min)
  ✅ Smaller shared surface than A
  ❌ Classifier, dead-letter handoff and log line are still copied five times, so most of the duplication and its tests remain
Net: One under-100-line module now, or five copies plus a promise.

options.label: One shared retry-policy module (recommended)
options.description: Small module: buildBackoff (base/multiplier/maxDelay/rng), classify (per-worker retryable/fatal lists), toDeadLetter (persist + metric), logAttempt, and startup config validation. All 5 workers use it with their own values. Human ~1 day / CC ~20 min. Completeness 10/10.

options.label: Five inline copies (as planned)
options.description: Each worker carries its own curve, classifier, dead-letter handoff and log line; refactor deferred. Human ~1.5 days / CC ~30 min. Completeness 4/10.

options.label: Extract curve builder only
options.description: Shared buildBackoff (jitter + cap) only; classifier, dead-letter handoff and log line stay inline in each of the 5 workers. Human ~1 day / CC ~15 min. Completeness 7/10.

questions.question:
D8 — How do we prove processWebhookJob() still sends each event at most once?
Project/branch/task: main branch, retry-framework plan; regression coverage for the rewritten webhook worker (D2 fixed the behavior to keep).
ELI10: The webhook worker is being rewritten and it carries a promise to receivers: an event is never sent twice. D2 kept that promise while adding retries for failures that happen before anything is sent. A rewrite with no test for the promise means the first duplicate email or double charge is found by a customer. The test is straightforward: a fake receiver counts sends, and we assert the count is exactly one across every failure pattern. The question is how deep to go: assertions against the worker alone, a run through the real library hooks, or both.
Stakes if we pick wrong: a retry path nobody tested sends duplicates to non-idempotent receivers, or a hook wiring mistake means pre-send failures never actually retry and the framework quietly does nothing for webhooks.
Recommendation: A because the unit layer pins each failure class cheaply and the integration layer is the only thing that catches hook wiring and attempt persistence, which is where retry bugs actually live.
Completeness: A=10/10, B=7/10, C=7/10
Pros / cons:
A) Unit + integration through the library hooks (recommended)
  ✅ Every failure class (pre-send, timeout, 5xx, reset, success) asserted in isolation with a recording fake transport (human: ~1 day / CC: ~20 min)
  ✅ One end-to-end run through the real hooks with a fake receiver catches wiring and attempt-persistence bugs the unit layer cannot see
  ❌ Two test layers to maintain; the integration test needs the library's test harness or an in-process queue
B) Unit tests only
  ✅ Fast, deterministic, no queue infrastructure in the test run (human: ~half day / CC: ~10 min)
  ✅ Pins the classifier and the send-count contract per failure class
  ❌ Never exercises the real hook registration, so a miswired hook passes tests and never retries in production
C) Integration test only
  ✅ Exercises the real path receivers depend on (human: ~half day / CC: ~10 min)
  ✅ Fewer tests to write
  ❌ Slower, and a failure tells you "something duplicated" without pointing at which failure class; edge classes get skipped for time
Net: Cheap isolated assertions plus one real-path run, versus trusting either layer alone to protect a promise made to external receivers.

options.label: Unit + integration (recommended)
options.description: Unit: fake transport records every send; assert exactly 1 send after pre-send retries, 0 further sends after timeout/5xx/reset with a dead-letter entry, 1 send on success. Integration: real library hooks + fake receiver, same assertions, plus attempt count survives a simulated worker restart. Human ~1 day / CC ~20 min. Completeness 10/10.

options.label: Unit tests only
options.description: The unit assertions from A against the worker with a fake transport; no run through the real library hooks. Human ~half day / CC ~10 min. Completeness 7/10.

options.label: Integration test only
options.description: The integration run from A only; no isolated per-failure-class assertions. Human ~half day / CC ~10 min. Completeness 7/10.

questions.question:
D9 — Cache the dependency graph across retries now, or measure first?
Project/branch/task: main branch, retry-framework plan; per-attempt cost inside the 5 workers running through library hooks (D1).
ELI10: The plan worries that each retry reloads the job and rebuilds its dependency graph from scratch. After D1 the reload is just the library handing the job to the worker, which happens anyway. The rebuild is real extra CPU, but only on retries, and D3 caps those at 5 per failing job. Storing the graph on the first attempt would add a write to every job, including the large majority that succeed first time, to save work on the few that fail. Nobody has measured how long the rebuild takes.
Stakes if we pick wrong: either we add a write and a staleness risk to every job to fix a cost nobody measured, or a genuinely slow rebuild keeps burning worker time on retries and we only find out under load.
Recommendation: C because an unmeasured optimization that taxes the happy path is the wrong trade; two timing metrics make the real decision cheap and data-driven.
Note: options differ in kind (persisted cache vs in-process memo vs measure first) — no completeness score.
Pros / cons:
A) Persist the graph with the job on attempt 1
  ✅ Retries never recompute; cost is paid once per job regardless of which worker instance retries (human: ~1 day / CC: ~20 min)
  ✅ Simple to reason about once the invalidation rule (payload version) is in place
  ❌ Adds a write and stored blob to every job, including the ones that never retry; stale-graph bugs if the payload changes between attempts
B) In-process memo (bounded LRU)
  ✅ No persistence, no schema change; a few lines around the graph builder (human: ~2 hr / CC: ~10 min)
  ✅ Zero cost on the happy path beyond a map insert
  ❌ Retries after a 10-minute delay usually land on a different worker instance, so the hit rate is low and unpredictable
C) Measure first: timing metrics + p95 budget (recommended)
  ✅ Two metrics (graph compute ms, payload bytes) per attempt tell you whether this is 2 ms or 2 s before anyone writes cache code (human: ~1 hr / CC: ~5 min)
  ✅ No happy-path cost, no staleness risk, and the retry-policy module already logs per attempt (D7) so the hook point exists
  ❌ If the rebuild is genuinely slow, retries stay expensive until the follow-up lands
Net: Add a write to every job to save CPU on the few that retry, or spend an hour on metrics and decide with numbers.

options.label: Persist the graph with the job
options.description: Compute once on attempt 1, store the graph beside the job row, reuse on retries, invalidate when the payload version changes. Adds a write to every job. Human ~1 day / CC ~20 min.

options.label: In-process memo (bounded LRU)
options.description: Memoize the graph per worker instance keyed by job id + payload hash, bounded LRU. No persistence; low hit rate when retries land on another instance. Human ~2 hr / CC ~10 min.

options.label: Measure first (recommended)
options.description: No cache. Add per-attempt timing metrics (job load ms, graph compute ms, payload bytes) via the retry-policy module's attempt log, set a p95 budget, and revisit caching with data. Human ~1 hr / CC ~5 min.

questions.question:
D10 — Track dead-letter retention as a TODO, skip it, or build it now?
Project/branch/task: main branch, retry-framework plan; follow-up to the dead-letter store approved in D3.
ELI10: The dead-letter store keeps every job that ran out of retries or hit a fatal error. Nothing ever removes them. That is fine for months, then the table is large, the growth alert query slows, and nobody remembers why. A purge job with a retention period fixes it, but the retention period is a judgment call about how long failed-job evidence must stay around.
Stakes if we pick wrong: build it now with the wrong retention and you delete evidence of lost work; skip it and the store becomes an unbounded table someone discovers during an incident.
Recommendation: A because the store is new, growth is slow, and the retention period deserves an owner's answer rather than a default picked inside a retry PR; the TODO carries a concrete trigger.
Completeness: A=6/10, B=2/10, C=10/10
Pros / cons:
A) Add to TODOS.md with a trigger (recommended)
  ✅ Keeps this PR right-sized: the retry framework ships without a retention debate attached
  ✅ Trigger (10k rows or 3 months) means the TODO fires before growth matters (human: ~5 min / CC: ~1 min now)
  ❌ Unbounded growth until someone acts on the TODO; the ceiling is a slow query, not data loss
B) Skip
  ✅ Nothing to track or build
  ✅ Zero effort now
  ❌ The store grows forever with no record that anyone considered it
C) Build now in this PR
  ✅ Store ships bounded from day one: purge job, 90-day default, keep flag, tests (human: ~2 hr / CC: ~10 min)
  ✅ No follow-up to forget
  ❌ Expands this PR with a scheduled job and a retention default nobody has agreed to; deletes evidence if the default is wrong
Net: A tracked follow-up with a trigger, versus a bigger PR that guesses how long failed-job evidence should live.

options.label: Add to TODOS.md (recommended)
options.description: Record the TODO (what/why/pros/cons/context/depends-on) with trigger: build when the dead-letter store passes 10k rows or at 3 months, whichever first. Human ~5 min / CC ~1 min. Completeness 6/10.

options.label: Skip — not valuable enough
options.description: Do not track retention. Completeness 2/10.

options.label: Build it now in this PR
options.description: Scheduled purge job, retention config default 90 days, keep flag, tests, shipped with the dead-letter store. Human ~2 hr / CC ~10 min. Completeness 10/10.

questions.question:
D11 — Track the webhook event-id header and at-least-once opt-in as a TODO, skip it, or ship the header now?
Project/branch/task: main branch, retry-framework plan; follow-up to D2 (webhook worker stays at-most-once).
ELI10: D2 kept the promise that a webhook is never sent twice, which means a send that times out is still lost. The usual fix is to stamp every event with a stable id so receivers can ignore duplicates, and then retry freely. That is a contract change, so it was declined for this PR. Question D4:
D4 — Should retry delays be randomized (jitter)?
Project/branch/task: main branch, retry-framework plan; the backoff curve each worker supplies to the library hooks (D1).
ELI10: When many jobs fail at the same moment because a shared dependency went down, a pure exponential curve makes them all retry at the same moments too, so the recovering dependency gets hit by a wave on every step.
